To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) for adults surviving stroke due spontaneous (non-traumatic) ICH, who had taken an antiplatelet drug for the prevention vaso-occlusive disease before the haemorrhage, starting antiplatelet drugs after ICH did not reduce the risks of recurrent haemorrhage or major haemorrhage compared to avoiding anti-platelet therapy.

In patients with a recent spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage, the risk of recurrent intracerebral bleeding was not increased with the initiation of antiplatelet therapy, but the rate of major ischemic vascular events was increased.

starting antiplatelet treatment after ICH due to antithrombotics was associated with a lower rate of recurrent stroke, but a higher rate of recurrent intracranial haemorrhage, and that the overall effect on major vascular events was neutral.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the question of whether starting antiplatelets for patients who have survived a stroke due to an intracerebral bleed and have taken antithrombotics for the prevention of vascular disease is safe and effective in terms of the risk of recurrent stroke, major haemorraghic events or a composite of major vascular events.

understanding how to best manage the use of antiplatelet drugs in people who have had a spontaneous (i.e. non traumatic) bleed in the brain due to the use of an antiplatelet drug, and who are at risk of a second bleed.

the question of whether or not to restart antiplatelet therapy (aspirin or clopidogrel or other) in patients who have had a brain haemorrhage caused by an antiplatelet drug (such as aspirin or clopidorel) and who have survived.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
RESTART is a randomised trial comparing two treatment strategies for adults surviving stroke due spontaneous (non traumatic intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) associated with antithrombotics.

the RESTART trial is a pragmatic, open-label, assessor-blind, parallel group randomised controlled trial of starting versus avoiding anti-platelet therapy in adults surviving spontaneous (i.e. non-traumatic) ICH.
the trial was well conducted with a low risk of bias and a low risk of missing important outcomes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are a large, multicentre, investigator initiated randomised trial of antithrombotics in patients with ICH.
we have shown that the use of antiplatelet therapy is safe in patients with ICH and is associated with a significant reduction in vascular events, particularly ischaemic stroke.

the RESTART trial is the largest randomised trial of antiplatelet therapy after spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage and that our findings will provide the best available information on the benefits and harms of this treatment.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the RESTART trial has been conducted according to the protocol, the data have been collected in the manner specified in the statistical analysis plan, and the analyses were carried out as described in this statistical analysis plan.
the results of the RESTART trial should be interpreted in the context of the patient's risk factors and the indication for antithrombotics before their intracerebral hemorrhage.
there is no clear benefit to starting antiplatelet drugs in patients who have survived an ICH.
